Mechanism Tissue-factor-driven thrombin generation → microthrombosis + consumption → bleeding Diagnosis ISTH score ≥ 5 (platelets, D-dimer, PT, fibrinogen); SIC score; serial tests Treatment Treat cause Bleeding: platelets < 50, FFP for long PT, fibrinogen if < 1.5 g/L Not bleeding: platelets only if < 10–20; heparin for thrombosis-predominant DIC Products treat bleeding, not numbers – the cause must be fixed.

Concept Uncontrolled macrophage/T-cell activation; triggers: EBV, lymphoma, autoimmune (MAS) Diagnosis HLH-2004 ≥ 5/8; ferritin often > 10 000; sCD25; HScore > 169; marrow biopsy Treatment Treat trigger; dexamethasone + etoposide (HLH-94) Anakinra for MAS/sepsis-like cases; IVIG; supportive care Culture-negative 'sepsis' with very high ferritin and cytopenias – think HLH.

Problems Neutropenic sepsis, CMV, fungi; SOS/VOD; engraftment syndrome, DAH, IPS; GVHD, TMA SOS/VOD Bilirubin ≥ 34, painful hepatomegaly, weight gain, ascites; reversed portal flow Defibrotide for severe; fluid and salt restriction, RRT Acute GVHD Skin, liver, gut grading; methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg; ruxolitinib if refractory Number of failing organs predicts ICU outcome after HSCT.

Definition Cairo–Bishop: ≥ 2 of high urate, K, PO4 or low Ca; clinical = plus AKI, arrhythmia, seizure Treatment Hydration 3 L/m²/day, UO > 100 mL/h Rasburicase (not in G6PD deficiency); allopurinol for prevention Treat high K; treat low Ca only if symptomatic; early RRT No urinary alkalinisation Promotes calcium phosphate precipitation; not needed with rasburicase Prevention starts before chemotherapy in high-risk tumours.

Causes Waldenström IgM, myeloma (IgA, IgG3), hyperleukocytosis, polycythaemia, cryoglobulins Features Mucosal bleeding, visual change ('sausage' veins), neurological symptoms, heart failure Treatment Plasmapheresis for paraprotein; leukapheresis + cytoreduction for leukostasis Avoid red cell transfusion until viscosity reduced; treat underlying disease Transfusing red cells can worsen hyperviscosity.

Causes Sepsis/DIC, dilution, drugs, HIT, ECMO/CRRT, TMA, liver disease, pseudothrombocytopenia HIT 4Ts score; PF4/heparin immunoassay; functional assay confirms HIT treatment Stop all heparin; argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or DOAC No warfarin until platelets > 150; no platelet transfusion; ≥ 3 months if thrombosis HIT is prothrombotic – stopping heparin alone is not enough.

Rebalanced haemostasis Low pro- and anticoagulant factors; high vWF; INR does not predict bleeding Assessment Viscoelastic tests; fibrinogen and platelets more useful than INR Procedures No routine FFP for INR; ultrasound guidance, experienced operator High-risk procedures/bleeding: platelets > 50, fibrinogen > 1.2–1.5 g/L Cirrhotic patients clot as well as bleed – still give VTE prophylaxis.

Assessment ATLS; FAST positive + unstable → theatre; stable → contrast CT Seatbelt sign: bowel, mesentery, Chance fracture Solid organ injury Non-operative management if stable; contrast blush → angioembolisation Serial exams; laparotomy if unstable/peritonitis; post-splenectomy vaccines Damage-control surgery Control bleeding and contamination, temporary closure, ICU resuscitation, return in 24–48 h Haemodynamic status, not injury grade, decides operation.

ATLS classes I < 15%; II 15–30% (tachycardia); III 30–40% (hypotension, confusion); IV > 40% Resuscitation Pressure/tourniquet; early blood (O-neg → MTP 1:1:1), TXA, permissive hypotension Prevent hypothermia and hypocalcaemia; viscoelastic testing Prehospital evidence PAMPer: prehospital plasma ↓ mortality; RePHILL: no benefit; whole blood evolving Haemorrhage control is the definitive resuscitation.

Definition LVEF < 45% late pregnancy to months postpartum, no other cause Risks: African ancestry, pre-eclampsia, multiple pregnancy, age, multiparity; 16-kDa prolactin Treatment Postpartum GDMT (enalapril safe in breastfeeding); no ACEi/ARNI in pregnancy Bromocriptine + anticoagulation (BOARD); anticoagulate if EF < 30–35%, thrombus or AF Shock: levosimendan, early MCS; avoid high-dose catecholamines; wearable defibrillator Prognosis ~50% recover by 6 months; future pregnancy risky if EF not normal Breathlessness postpartum needs an echo, not just reassurance.

Presentation Labour/within 30 min postpartum: sudden hypoxia, hypotension/arrest, DIC Biphasic: RV failure from pulmonary hypertension, then LV failure Resuscitation ALS with uterine displacement; resuscitative hysterotomy within 5 min if ≥ 20 weeks RV support (noradrenaline, inotropes, inhaled vasodilators), avoid overload Aggressive fibrinogen, FFP, platelets, TXA; viscoelastic testing; VA-ECMO Diagnosis Clinical exclusion: PE, anaphylaxis, haemorrhage, eclampsia, high spinal, LA toxicity Expect coagulopathy early and prepare products at once.

Physiology ↑ minute ventilation; normal PaCO2 ≈ 4.0 kPa; ↓ FRC, ↑ O2 consumption → fast desaturation Airway oedema, aspiration risk Airway Experienced operator, ramp, uterine displacement, HFNO/NIV pre-oxygenation RSI, smaller tube, videolaryngoscope, obstetric difficult airway plan Ventilation targets SpO2 ≥ 95% (PaO2 > 9.3–10 kPa); PaCO2 4.0–4.7 kPa Lung-protective ventilation; prone and ECMO feasible; delivery may help A 'normal' PaCO2 of 5.3 kPa is hypercapnia in late pregnancy.

Definitions Hypertension after 20 weeks + proteinuria or organ dysfunction Severe: BP ≥ 160/110, low platelets, liver/renal failure, pulmonary oedema, neuro signs HELLP = haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets Management Magnesium 4 g load + 1 g/h × 24 h (MAGPIE); extra 2 g for recurrence; watch reflexes/RR BP < 150/100: IV labetalol, hydralazine, oral nifedipine Delivery after stabilisation; fluid restriction ~80 mL/h Complications ICH, PRES, pulmonary oedema, AKI, liver haematoma/rupture, DIC, abruption Magnesium prevents seizures; antihypertensives prevent strokes.

4 Ts Tone (70%), trauma, tissue, thrombin Management Massage, oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol TXA 1 g within 3 h (WOMAN); early fibrinogen (keep > 2 g/L), FIBTEM-guided Balloon tamponade, B-Lynch, embolisation, hysterectomy Fibrinogen < 2 g/L predicts severe PPH; falls earlier than other factors Call for help early and run treatments in parallel.

Recognition Physiological tachycardia, low BP, raised WBC mask sepsis; use MEOWS/omqSOFA; lactate valid Sources Endometritis, chorioamnionitis, septic abortion, wound, mastitis, pyelonephritis, pneumonia Group A strep can kill within hours Management Hour-1 bundle; pip-taz + clindamycin for GAS Source control (retained products, debridement, hysterectomy); IVIG for toxic shock Fetal monitoring and timing of delivery with obstetrics Diarrhoea and severe pain postpartum may be group A streptococcus.

Mechanisms Na-channel block (wide QRS, VT), alpha-block (hypotension), anticholinergic, GABA-A block (seizures) ECG risk QRS > 100 ms seizures, > 160 ms arrhythmia; R in aVR > 3 mm Treatment Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg repeated to pH 7.45–7.55; hyperventilate if intubated Benzodiazepines for seizures (no phenytoin); avoid physostigmine Noradrenaline; lidocaine for VT; charcoal if airway safe; lipid/ECMO for arrest Bicarbonate is the antidote – titrate to QRS narrowing.

boxes.t: Ch 7 · Beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker poisoning
boxes.x: Features Bradycardia, AV block, hypotension; CCB: hyperglycaemia; BB: hypoglycaemia, bronchospasm Propranolol: seizures, wide QRS; sotalol: long QT Treatment Charcoal; whole bowel irrigation for slow-release IV calcium; high-dose insulin 1 U/kg then 1–10 U/kg/h with glucose Noradrenaline/adrenaline, pacing; lipid, methylene blue, VA-ECMO; glucagon for BB Hyperglycaemia severity tracks CCB poisoning severity.

Agents Cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA, cathinones, synthetic cannabinoids MDMA: hyponatraemia from ADH + water intake Management Benzodiazepines generously; rapid cooling (ice water) to < 39 °C Hypertension: phentolamine/nitrates; avoid pure beta blockers with cocaine 3% saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia; fluids for rhabdomyolysis Complications ACS, stroke, dissection, AKI, DIC, compartment syndrome Hyperthermia kills – cool first, antipyretics do not work.

boxes.t: Ch 9 · Ethylene glycol and toxic alcohols
boxes.x: Labs High anion gap acidosis + high osmolar gap; oxalate crystals Toxicity ADH → glycolate (acidosis) → oxalate (AKI, low Ca); methanol → formate (blindness) Treatment Fomepizole (or ethanol) Haemodialysis: pH < 7.25, AKI, high levels, visual/neuro signs (EXTRIP) Bicarbonate; thiamine + pyridoxine (EG), folate (methanol) Osmolar gap falls as the toxic acids rise – a normal gap late does not exclude it.

Classification SJS < 10% BSA; overlap 10–30%; TEN > 30% Drugs: allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides, nevirapine SCORTEN Age > 40, malignancy, HR > 120, BSA > 10%, urea > 10, HCO3 < 20, glucose > 14 Management Stop drug; burns unit; warm room, fluids, nutrition, analgesia Non-adherent dressings, eye care (ophthalmology), mucosal care Immunomodulation (ciclosporin, etanercept, IVIG) – uncertain evidence Stopping the culprit drug early is the most effective treatment.

Timeline 6–24 h tremor; 6–48 h seizures; 12–48 h hallucinosis; 48–96 h delirium tremens Treatment Benzodiazepines: symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar) or front-loading IV thiamine before glucose; Mg, K, PO4, fluids Refractory: phenobarbital, propofol; dexmedetomidine adjunct only Wernicke's Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; high-dose IV thiamine; untreated → Korsakoff Antipsychotics alone lower seizure threshold – benzodiazepines first.

Team benefits Multidisciplinary rounds ↓ mortality; pharmacist ↓ drug errors; checklists improve compliance Communication and safety SBAR / I-PASS handover; daily goals Psychological safety: speak-up culture (CUS, two-challenge rule) Crew resource management, simulation, blame-free incident learning Burnout Exhaustion, depersonalisation, low accomplishment; moral distress Debriefing, ethics support, staffing, involvement in decisions Most ICU errors are communication failures.

Principles Respect wishes/advance directives; best interests if no capacity Shared decisions; no duty to give non-beneficial treatment; withholding = withdrawing Managing conflict Family meeting (VALUE), explore patient's values, honest prognosis Time-limited trial; second opinion; ethics/legal route if needed; document Withdrawal process Comfort-focused opioids/benzodiazepines (double effect) Terminal extubation or wean; family presence; organ donation referral; bereavement support The question is what the patient would want, not what the family wants.

Models Integrative (ICU team) and consultative (specialist triggers) Triggers: advanced cancer, ICU stay > 10 days, multiorgan failure, conflict Symptom control Pain (opioids + adjuvants), dyspnoea (opioids, fan), delirium, nausea, secretions Psychological and spiritual support Goals of care Ask–tell–ask; realistic outcomes; ceilings of care; revisit often Palliative care runs alongside active treatment, not after it.

Benefits Better trust and decisions; less anxiety/PTSD in relatives; helps prevent delirium Strategies Open visiting, participation in rounds and care, early family conference (≤ 72 h) ICU diaries, written information, interpreters, consistent communicator Presence during CPR Fewer PTSD symptoms in relatives (Jabre 2013); no effect on CPR quality with a support person Families are part of the care team, not visitors.

Domains Physical (weakness, fatigue), cognitive (memory, attention), mental (anxiety, depression, PTSD) PICS-F in family members Risk factors Delirium, sepsis, ARDS, long ventilation, deep sedation, benzodiazepines, immobility, frailty Prevention and recovery ABCDEF bundle, early mobility, family engagement; ICU diaries ↓ PTSD Follow-up clinics, rehabilitation, return-to-work and peer support Survival is not the only outcome – plan recovery from day one.

boxes.t: Sepsis-3, severity scores and the Hour-1 bundle
boxes.x: Definitions Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection; SOFA rise ≥ 2 Septic shock = vasopressor for MAP ≥ 65 and lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid Sepsis-2: SIRS ≥ 2 + infection; 'severe sepsis' abolished; SIRS sensitive but non-specific Scores qSOFA (RR ≥ 22, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100): prognostic only; SSC 2021 advises against it as sole screen NEWS2/MEWS: best for early deterioration; SOFA = diagnosis/trend; APACHE II (24 h) = mortality prediction Hour-1 bundle Lactate (repeat if > 2) · blood cultures ×2 · broad IV antibiotics < 1 h 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid if hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 · noradrenaline if MAP < 65 Look for source early (CT, ultrasound) and control it Scores support, never replace, clinical judgement; time to antibiotics matters most in shock.

Vasopressors Noradrenaline first line, peripheral start acceptable; target MAP ≥ 65 (60–65 acceptable if ≥ 65 yr: 65 trial) Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min when NA 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min (VASST: benefit in less severe shock) Then adrenaline; dobutamine if low CO with myocardial dysfunction; angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) option Corticosteroids Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if NA/adr ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min ≥ 4 h (SSC 2021) ADRENAL: faster shock reversal, no mortality change; APROCCHSS (+ fludrocortisone): ↓ 90-day mortality Perfusion and beta-blockade Low ScvO2 + high lactate → inadequate DO2: check Hb, CO, fluid response Esmolol/landiolol for persistent tachycardia > 95 after resuscitation: Morelli 2013 positive, STRESS-L harm signal Escalate in steps, review every hour: MAP, perfusion, lactate clearance, CRT.

boxes.t: ROSE fluid model, VExUS and de-resuscitation
boxes.x: ROSE phases Rescue (bolus, minutes) → Optimisation (titrate to responsiveness) → Stabilisation (maintain, zero balance) → Evacuation (de-resuscitate) Fluid is a drug: give only if responsive and still hypoperfused VExUS (venous congestion) Start with IVC > 2 cm; grade hepatic, portal and intrarenal venous Doppler Grade 0 none · 1 mild · 2 one severely abnormal · 3 ≥ 2 severely abnormal → predicts AKI De-resuscitation and fluid choice Diuretics or CRRT ultrafiltration; targets: negative balance, falling weight, EVLW, IAP Balanced crystalloids ≥ saline (SMART); albumin if large volumes (ALBIOS subgroup); avoid HES (6S, CHEST) CLASSIC, CLOVERS: restrictive ≈ liberal fluids Positive balance after day 3 is linked with mortality: plan evacuation early.

boxes.t: Oxygen delivery, ScvO2 and CO2 gap
boxes.x: Oxygen delivery DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10; CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2 (kPa ×0.023) Normal DO2 ≈ 1000 mL/min (550–650 mL/min/m²); VO2 ≈ 250 mL/min; O2ER 20–30% Venous markers ScvO2 < 70%: low DO2 or high VO2; high ScvO2 (> 80%) may mean shunting/impaired extraction Pcv–aCO2 gap > 6 mmHg = low flow even if ScvO2 normal; gap/C(a–v)O2 ratio > 1.4 = anaerobic metabolism Lactate: type A (hypoperfusion) vs type B (adrenaline, liver failure, metformin) Improving tissue oxygenation Raise CO (fluid if responsive, dobutamine), Hb if < 7 (or ischaemia), SaO2 Reduce VO2: sedation, ventilation, cooling fever, control shivering Normal ScvO2 does not exclude hypoperfusion: always add the CO2 gap and lactate.

Definition and types Shock = circulatory failure causing inadequate cellular O2 use; lactate > 2 mmol/L Hypovolaemic and cardiogenic: low CO, high SVR; obstructive: low CO, high CVP; distributive: high CO, low SVR Ultrasound (RUSH / pump-tank-pipes) Pump: LV function, RV dilatation, effusion/tamponade Tank: IVC size/collapse, FAST, pleural fluid, B-lines (lung oedema) Pipes: aortic aneurysm/dissection, DVT Resuscitation targets MAP ≥ 65, CRT normal (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK), UO > 0.5 mL/kg/h, lactate falling Treatment follows type: fluids/blood, inotrope, decompression/drainage/lysis, vasopressor + source control Classify early with ultrasound; the shock type decides the treatment.

Immediate management Stop trigger, call help, lie flat/legs up, high-flow O2 IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 min Fluid 500–1000 mL bolus; refractory: IV adrenaline infusion 0.05–0.1 µg/kg/min Airway oedema: early intubation by expert; nebulised adrenaline as a bridge Beta-blocked patient Bisoprolol blunts adrenaline response → refractory hypotension, bradycardia Glucagon 1–5 mg IV over 5 min, then 5–15 µg/min infusion; vasopressin/NA if needed Confirmation and follow-up Mast-cell tryptase at ≈ 1 h and 2–4 h, baseline at 24 h Antihistamines/steroids are second-line only; observe 6–12 h (biphasic risk) Allergy referral, adrenaline auto-injector, report the reaction Adrenaline IM is the only first-line drug; never delay it for antihistamines.

boxes.t: Vitamin C, adjuncts and post-sepsis syndrome
boxes.x: Vitamin C evidence Marik 2017 (HAT, before–after) positive; VITAMINS, ACTS, VICTAS neutral LOVIT 2022: high-dose vitamin C ↑ death or persistent organ dysfunction → not recommended (SSC 2021) Other adjuncts Hydrocortisone in refractory shock: yes · IVIG, selenium, statins, polymyxin B haemoperfusion: no Bicarbonate only if pH ≤ 7.2 + AKI (BICAR-ICU); blood purification: research only Insulin target 8–10 mmol/L (NICE-SUGAR) Post-sepsis syndrome Physical weakness, cognitive impairment, PTSD/depression, recurrent infection, readmission Follow-up clinic, rehabilitation, medication review, family support, ICU diaries Most sepsis 'magic bullets' failed; good basic care and follow-up improve outcome.

Definitions Fever: raised hypothalamic set point (cytokines, PGE2), responds to antipyretics Hyperthermia: set point normal, heat production/loss failure (NMS, MH, serotonin, heat stroke); antipyretics useless Causes of fever in ICU Infective: VAP, CRBSI, UTI, sinusitis, C. difficile, surgical site, abscess Non-infective: drugs, DVT/PE, pancreatitis, transfusion, acalculous cholecystitis, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, CNS bleed Work-up and treatment Exam, lines, cultures (blood ×2, sample site), CXR, imaging of source; PCT trend Paracetamol for comfort; HEAT/REACTOR: no mortality benefit from treating fever Active cooling for hyperthermia and after brain injury/cardiac arrest (avoid > 37.7) Fever > 41 °C or no response to antipyretics → think hyperthermia syndrome.

PK changes ↑ Volume of distribution (capillary leak, fluids, ECMO) → higher loading dose Augmented renal clearance (CrCl > 130) → underdosing; AKI/CRRT alter clearance Low albumin ↑ free fraction of highly bound drugs (ceftriaxone, teicoplanin) PK/PD targets Time-dependent (beta-lactams): fT > MIC → extended/continuous infusion (BLING III, MERINO) Concentration-dependent (aminoglycosides): Cmax/MIC 8–10 → once daily AUC/MIC: vancomycin (AUC 400–600), quinolones TDM and stewardship TDM for vancomycin, aminoglycosides, and beta-lactams where available (TARGET) Full loading dose regardless of renal function; adjust maintenance only Early full loading + prolonged beta-lactam infusion = right drug, right dose.

Stewardship principles Right drug, dose, route, timing, duration; cultures before antibiotics Daily review: 48–72 h 'time-out', de-escalate by culture, switch IV → oral Local antibiogram, restricted lists, ID/microbiology input, audit and feedback Procalcitonin Stop when PCT < 0.5 µg/L or ≥ 80% fall from peak (SAPS: ↓ duration and mortality, PRORATA) Not for starting antibiotics in shock; false rise in surgery, trauma, burns, pancreatitis Duration 7 days for most (VAP, intra-abdominal after source control: STOP-IT 4 days) Uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteraemia 7 days (BALANCE: 7 = 14) Longer: S. aureus bacteraemia, endocarditis, undrained abscess, osteomyelitis Shorter courses are as good and reduce resistance and C. difficile.

Risk factors Prior antibiotics within 90 days, long ICU stay, MV, devices, previous colonisation Travel/hospital in high-prevalence area, dialysis, nursing home, immunosuppression Empirical choice (local ecology) ESBL: carbapenem (MERINO: meropenem > pip-taz) CRE (KPC/OXA-48): ceftazidime-avibactam; MBL (NDM): ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam CRAB: colistin or sulbactam-durlobactam combinations; CR Pseudomonas: ceftolozane-tazobactam Colistin: loading 9 MU, nephrotoxic; combine and de-escalate once sensitivities known Infection control Contact precautions, single room/cohorting, hand hygiene, screening swabs Chlorhexidine bathing, environmental cleaning, stewardship Know your antibiogram: the empirical regimen depends on local resistance.

Definitions CLABSI: surveillance, BSI with CVC > 48 h, no other source CRBSI: clinical, catheter proven as source: DTP ≥ 2 h (catheter culture positive ≥ 2 h earlier) or same organism on tip (≥ 15 CFU) Management Remove line if: S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, tunnel/pocket infection, shock, persistent bacteraemia Empirical vancomycin ± Gram-negative cover; duration 7–14 days; S. aureus ≥ 14 days + echo Lock therapy only for long-term lines with CoNS when removal impossible Prevention bundle Hand hygiene, maximal barrier, chlorhexidine 2% in alcohol, subclavian preferred, ultrasound Daily review, remove unneeded lines, chlorhexidine dressings Persistent bacteraemia after 72 h → think endocarditis or septic thrombosis.

boxes.t: Peritonitis, source control and abdominal hypertension
boxes.x: Classification Primary (SBP), secondary (perforation/leak), tertiary (persistent after adequate treatment) Tertiary: immunosuppression, resistant flora (Enterococcus, Candida, CoNS), high mortality Source control Drain, debride, divert, restore: within 6–12 h; percutaneous drainage if possible Damage control laparotomy if unstable; relook if needed Intra-abdominal hypertension IAH ≥ 12 mmHg; ACS > 20 + new organ failure; APP = MAP − IAP (target ≥ 60) Decompress (NGT, rectal tube), drain ascites, sedation/NMB, negative balance, laparostomy Antibiotics Pip-taz or carbapenem; add antifungal and anti-enterococcal cover in tertiary peritonitis 4 days after source control (STOP-IT) Antibiotics fail without source control: drain early.

Risk factors Broad antibiotics, CVC, TPN, abdominal surgery/leak, pancreatitis, dialysis Multifocal colonisation (Candida score ≥ 3), immunosuppression, long ICU stay Diagnosis Blood cultures ≈ 50% sensitive; beta-D-glucan (high NPV, false positives: albumin, IVIG, dialysis) Mannan/anti-mannan, T2Candida PCR; eye exam and echo if candidaemia Treatment Echinocandin first line (caspofungin, anidulafungin, micafungin) Step-down to fluconazole if sensitive and stable; remove CVC 14 days after first negative culture and resolution Strategy Prophylaxis: high-risk without infection (e.g. recurrent leak) Pre-emptive: biomarker/colonisation guided; empirical: septic shock with risk factors Candidaemia is never a contaminant: treat, remove the line, look for endophthalmitis.

Risk factors Neutropenia, haematological malignancy, HSCT, solid organ transplant, high-dose steroids ICU: COPD on steroids, cirrhosis, severe influenza (IAPA) or COVID-19 (CAPA) Diagnosis CT: nodules, halo sign (early), air-crescent (late); wedge infarcts BAL galactomannan (> 1.0), serum galactomannan (neutropenic), Aspergillus PCR, culture EORTC/MSG (host + clinical + mycology); AspICU for non-neutropenic ICU patients Treatment Voriconazole (or isavuconazole) first line; liposomal amphotericin if azole resistant TDM for voriconazole (1–5.5 mg/L); visual disturbance, hepatotoxicity, QT Interactions: CYP3A4 inhibition (tacrolimus, ciclosporin); 6–12 weeks Influenza patients deteriorating in ICU: send BAL galactomannan.

Diagnosis Fever, loin pain, pyuria; complicated if obstruction, male, catheter, pregnancy, diabetes Emphysematous pyelonephritis: gas on CT, diabetics (Huang–Tseng classes 1–4) Management Cultures, broad antibiotics (cephalosporin/pip-taz; carbapenem if ESBL risk) Imaging for obstruction → urgent decompression (nephrostomy or stent) Emphysematous: drainage, nephrectomy for extensive disease CAUTI prevention Avoid unnecessary catheters; remove early (nurse-led protocols) Aseptic insertion, closed drainage, bag below bladder; treat only symptomatic bacteriuria Obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency: drain it.

Severity (IDSA/IWGDF) Mild: local skin; moderate: deeper or > 2 cm erythema; severe: SIRS/systemic signs Assess pulses, ABPI, probe-to-bone (osteomyelitis), X-ray/MRI Microbiology Polymicrobial: S. aureus, streptococci, Gram-negatives, anaerobes; MRSA/Pseudomonas risks Management Glycaemic control, fluids, broad antibiotics (pip-taz ± vancomycin) Urgent surgical debridement of abscess, gas, necrosis; amputation if needed Vascular assessment and revascularisation; offloading; wound care Poor outcome predictors PAD/ischaemia, sepsis, osteomyelitis, high HbA1c, CKD, wet gangrene, delay Severe diabetic foot = sepsis + surgery: debride early.

Definition and first hour Neutrophils < 0.5 ×10^9/L (or falling) + temperature ≥ 38.3 once or ≥ 38 for 1 h Cultures, then anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam within 1 h (pip-taz, meropenem if ESBL) Add vancomycin for line infection, MRSA, skin/soft tissue, shock Antifungals Persistent fever after 4–7 days of antibiotics → CT chest, galactomannan Empirical/pre-emptive echinocandin or liposomal amphotericin; voriconazole for mould Complications Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis): CT, bowel rest, cover anaerobes, surgery if perforation Tumour lysis, mucositis, Pneumocystis, CMV G-CSF and outcome G-CSF not routine for established FN; consider in high-risk/sepsis Mortality ↑ with shock, MV, invasive fungal infection Antibiotics within 60 minutes save lives in neutropenic sepsis.

Modified Duke criteria Major: typical organism in 2 cultures, echo evidence (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation) Minor: predisposition, fever ≥ 38, vascular, immunological phenomena, atypical microbiology Definite: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor Antibiotics Empirical: vancomycin + gentamicin (native) or + rifampicin (prosthetic) MSSA: flucloxacillin/cefazolin; streptococci: penicillin/ceftriaxone; 4–6 weeks Urgent surgery Heart failure from valve dysfunction (emergency), uncontrolled infection/abscess Embolism prevention: vegetation > 10 mm with embolic event ICU complications Heart failure, emboli (stroke, spleen, kidney), mycotic aneurysm, AKI, heart block New heart block in endocarditis = root abscess until proven otherwise.

Classification Type I polymicrobial (diabetes, perineum: Fournier's); type II group A strep ± S. aureus Type III Clostridium/Vibrio; type IV fungal Diagnosis Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae, crepitus, shock LRINEC ≥ 6 suggests (poor sensitivity); CT gas/fascial fluid; surgery is diagnostic Management Urgent wide debridement, relook in 24 h Pip-taz/carbapenem + clindamycin (toxin suppression) ± vancomycin/linezolid IVIG for streptococcal TSS (considered); HBO not a delay Streptococcal toxic shock Hypotension + ≥ 2 organ failures with group A strep; rash, desquamation Source control, clindamycin, supportive care Never wait for imaging when NSTI is suspected clinically.

Severity features (P. falciparum) Impaired consciousness, seizures, shock, ARDS, AKI, acidosis, hypoglycaemia Parasitaemia > 10%, Hb < 7, jaundice, bleeding, haemoglobinuria Specific treatment IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h, then daily (AQUAMAT, SEAQUAMAT) Switch to oral ACT after ≥ 24 h when able; quinine only if no artesunate Watch delayed haemolysis 1–3 weeks later Supportive care Cautious fluids (FEAST: boluses harmful in children), glucose monitoring Treat seizures, RRT early, ventilation, transfusion; antibiotics for co-infection No steroids, mannitol or heparin; exchange transfusion not recommended Artesunate beats quinine: start it without delay.

Classification (WHO 2009) Dengue without/with warning signs; severe dengue (plasma leak shock, bleeding, organ failure) Warning signs: abdominal pain, vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleed, lethargy, liver ↑, rising HCT + falling platelets Phases Febrile (2–7 d) → critical (defervescence, 24–48 h leak) → recovery (reabsorption) Fluids in shock Crystalloid 10–20 mL/kg boluses guided by HCT and perfusion; taper over 24–48 h Colloid if refractory; rising HCT = more leak, falling HCT + instability = bleeding → blood Stop fluids in recovery phase (overload risk) Platelets Transfuse only for active bleeding or procedures; not prophylactic The danger comes when the fever falls: watch the critical phase closely.

Diagnosis Exposure to water/rats (floods, farmers); fever, myalgia (calves), conjunctival suffusion Weil's disease: jaundice + AKI + bleeding; pulmonary haemorrhage = worst Tests: PCR (first week), IgM ELISA, MAT; low K AKI (non-oliguric) Management Penicillin G or ceftriaxone IV; doxycycline for mild Supportive: early RRT, lung-protective ventilation, ECMO for haemorrhage Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction possible Differentials Malaria, dengue, hantavirus, typhoid, viral hepatitis, rickettsia, sepsis Fever + jaundice + AKI after flood exposure = leptospirosis.

Pathophysiology Autoinfection cycle; steroids/HTLV-1/transplant → hyperinfection and dissemination Larvae carry gut bacteria → Gram-negative bacteraemia and meningitis Diagnosis Eosinophilia (often absent in hyperinfection), larvae in stool, sputum or BAL Serology (IgG), agar plate culture, PCR Treatment and prevention Ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily until negative for 2 weeks; SC/rectal if no gut absorption Treat Gram-negative sepsis; reduce immunosuppression Screen/treat before steroids in endemic patients (e.g. Nile Delta) Gram-negative sepsis on steroids from an endemic area → check for Strongyloides.

Severity CURB-65 ≥ 3 severe; PSI class IV–V IDSA/ATS major: septic shock on vasopressors or invasive ventilation; minor ≥ 3 (RR ≥ 30, P/F ≤ 250, multilobar, confusion, urea ≥ 20, WBC < 4, platelets < 100, T < 36, hypotension) Microbiology Blood + sputum cultures, urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, viral PCR, MRSA nasal swab Antibiotics: beta-lactam + macrolide (or respiratory quinolone); MRSA/Pseudomonas cover only if risk Corticosteroids CAPE COD 2023: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 8–14 days ↓ 28-day mortality in severe CAP Avoid in influenza; benefit less clear in shock already on steroids Complications ARDS, septic shock, empyema, abscess, AKI, MI/arrhythmia, AF Severe CAP: severity → right antibiotics in 1 h → steroids → protect the lung.

boxes.t: HAP and VAP: diagnosis and treatment
boxes.x: Definitions HAP: pneumonia ≥ 48 h after admission; VAP: ≥ 48 h after intubation Diagnosis: new infiltrate + 2 of fever, purulent secretions, leucocytosis, worse oxygenation (CPIS > 6 supportive) Sampling Non-invasive semi-quantitative ETA (≥ 10⁵ CFU/mL) or BAL (≥ 10⁴); mini-BAL; before antibiotics Empirical antibiotics Anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (pip-taz, cefepime, meropenem) Add MRSA cover (vancomycin/linezolid) if MRSA > 10–20% or prior MRSA Second anti-Gram-negative agent if septic shock, prior IV antibiotics in 90 days, high resistance Duration 7 days for most; de-escalate by culture; PCT helps stopping Sample first, cover broadly, then narrow and stop at 7 days.

boxes.t: VAP prevention, SDD and oral care
boxes.x: Mechanical and positioning Head up 30–45°, cuff pressure 20–30 cmH2O, subglottic secretion drainage Avoid circuit changes unless soiled, closed suction, early tracheostomy not for VAP alone Selective digestive decontamination Topical non-absorbable antibiotics (oropharynx + gut) ± short IV cefotaxime SuDDICU 2022: no significant mortality fall; lower bacteraemia; resistance concern in high-MDR settings Other strategies Daily sedation holds and SBT, early extubation; avoid reintubation Chlorhexidine oral care: possible harm → toothbrushing preferred Stress-ulcer prophylaxis only if indicated (PPI ↑ pneumonia), probiotics not recommended The best prevention is shortening ventilation.

boxes.t: ARDS: Berlin definition and lung-protective care
boxes.x: Berlin definition Within 1 week; bilateral opacities; not fully explained by cardiac failure/overload PaO2/FiO2 on PEEP ≥ 5: mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe ≤ 100 (2023 global: SpO2/FiO2, HFNC) Phases Exudative (days 1–7: hyaline membranes, oedema) → proliferative → fibrotic Lung-protective ventilation Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤ 30, driving pressure ≤ 15 (ARMA) PEEP by FiO2 table or best compliance; conservative fluids (FACTT) Prone ≥ 16 h if P/F < 150 (PROSEVA); NMB not routine (ROSE) Pharmacology Dexamethasone (DEXA-ARDS) considered; no benefit from statins, beta-agonists, surfactant Keep driving pressure low: it predicts survival best.

Prone physiology and evidence More homogeneous ventilation, recruits dorsal lung, better V/Q, less overdistension, RV unloading PROSEVA: P/F < 150, ≥ 16 h/day → 28-day mortality 16% vs 33% Practice and complications Trained team (5–6), ETT secured, eyes/face/pressure areas, lines, feeding Complications: tube dislodgement, pressure sores, facial oedema, brachial plexus injury VV-ECMO criteria (EOLIA) P/F < 50 for 3 h, < 80 for 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO2 ≥ 60 for 6 h despite optimal care EOLIA: 35% vs 46% (NS), Bayesian reanalysis favours ECMO; CESAR: referral to centre Contraindications and outcome Relative: MV > 7 days, irreversible disease, contraindication to anticoagulation, severe brain injury RESP score predicts survival Prone first; refer to an ECMO centre early when criteria approach.

Blood gas Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis: pH < 7.35, PaCO2 high, raised HCO3 Cause: V/Q mismatch, ↑ dead space, muscle fatigue, dynamic hyperinflation NIV Indication: pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa despite medical therapy Contraindications: arrest, coma, vomiting, facial trauma, undrained pneumothorax, copious secretions Start IPAP 15 (up to 20–25), EPAP 4–5; recheck ABG 1–2 h; failure → intubate Pharmacology Nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, prednisolone 40 mg 5 days, antibiotics if purulent sputum Target SpO2 88–92% If intubated Low RR, long expiratory time, avoid auto-PEEP, permissive hypercapnia, early NIV after extubation NIV reduces intubation and mortality in hypercapnic AECOPD.

Features Life-threatening: PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, arrhythmia, normal/raised PaCO2 Near-fatal: raised PaCO2 and/or need for ventilation Hypotension after intubation Dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP) ± tension pneumothorax, hypovolaemia, sedatives Disconnect from ventilator for 30–60 s, chest compression, fluid, check for pneumothorax Ventilator strategy Low RR (8–10), Vt 6–8 mL/kg, I:E 1:4–5, high inspiratory flow Plateau < 30, measure auto-PEEP, accept PaCO2 high if pH > 7.2 Drugs and rescue Salbutamol, ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone, IV magnesium 2 g Ketamine, aminophylline, adrenaline, volatile anaesthetics, ECCO2R/ECMO In ventilated asthma, the key setting is a long expiratory time.

boxes.t: HFNO, ROX index and intubation timing
boxes.x: HFNO physiology Flow up to 60 L/min, FiO2 to 1.0; washes dead space, small PEEP, humidification, less work of breathing FLORALI: ↓ 90-day mortality vs NIV/standard O2 in de novo hypoxaemia ROX index ROX = (SpO2/FiO2) / RR ≥ 4.88 at 2, 6, 12 h predicts success; < 3.85 high failure risk → intubate Delayed intubation risks P-SILI from large swings, fatigue, emergency intubation, higher mortality (Kang 2015) Safe intubation plan Preoxygenation with HFNO/NIV, RSI, video laryngoscope, fluids + vasopressor ready Experienced operator, checklist, apnoeic oxygenation Reassess HFNO with ROX: don't let failing patients drift.

Light's criteria (exudate if any) Fluid/serum protein > 0.5; fluid/serum LDH > 0.6; fluid LDH > 2/3 upper normal serum Parapneumonic: simple → complicated (pH < 7.2, glucose < 3.3 mmol/L, LDH > 1000) → empyema (pus) Management Ultrasound-guided sampling; chest drain for complicated effusion/empyema Antibiotics with anaerobic cover; intrapleural tPA + DNase (MIST-2); VATS if failing Causes Transudate: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic, hypoalbuminaemia, PD Exudate: pneumonia, malignancy, PE, TB, pancreatitis, autoimmune pH < 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion means drain it.

Definition and danger > 200–600 mL/24 h or any amount causing airway compromise or instability Death from asphyxia, not blood loss; bronchial arteries (systemic pressure) bleed in 90% Immediate management Lie bleeding side down, high-flow O2, large-bore access, correct coagulation, TXA Intubate with large tube (≥ 8); single-lung intubation or bronchial blocker to isolate Definitive work-up CT angiography to locate; bronchoscopy for localisation and local therapy Bronchial artery embolisation first-line; surgery for failure or localised lesion Causes: bronchiectasis, TB, cancer, aspergilloma, vasculitis, PE Protect the good lung first: position and isolate.

boxes.t: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pulmonary–renal syndrome
boxes.x: Diagnosis Haemoptysis (may be absent), falling Hb, diffuse infiltrates, hypoxaemia BAL: progressively bloodier aliquots, haemosiderin-laden macrophages Pulmonary–renal: ANCA vasculitis (GPA, MPA), anti-GBM (Goodpasture), SLE Investigations ANCA (PR3, MPO), anti-GBM, ANA/dsDNA, complement, urine microscopy, renal biopsy Coagulation, echo, infection screen Management High-dose methylprednisolone 1 g/day × 3 then cyclophosphamide or rituximab Plasma exchange for anti-GBM; considered in severe ANCA (PEXIVAS: no overall benefit) Lung-protective ventilation, RRT, correct coagulation, ECMO if refractory Blood in the lungs + active urine sediment = pulmonary–renal syndrome.

Differences Pneumonitis (Mendelson): chemical injury from gastric acid, witnessed, rapid onset in hours Pneumonia: oropharyngeal bacteria, dysphagia, slower onset, infiltrates in dependent segments Antibiotics Not for pneumonitis in first 48 h unless SBO/gut obstruction or not resolving For pneumonia: amoxicillin-clavulanate or ceftriaxone; anaerobic cover not routine Stop meropenem/vancomycin if no risk factors (stewardship) Supportive care and prevention Suction, O2, NIV/ventilation, no steroids Swallow assessment, head-up, oral care, avoid sedatives Witnessed aspiration with rapid hypoxia is usually chemical: watch before treating.

Definition Acute worsening < 1 month with new bilateral ground-glass on HRCT, not explained by heart failure/fluid Triggers: infection, aspiration, surgery, drugs, PE Management Exclude infection, heart failure, PE; supportive O2/HFNO High-dose steroids commonly used (weak evidence); antifibrotics continued Mechanical ventilation: hospital mortality > 80–90%; only as bridge to transplant Goals of care Early honest discussion: prognosis, ventilation limits, palliative care, DNACPR Patient's values and wishes, family involvement AE-IPF has a poor prognosis: plan ceilings of care early.

Physiology EtCO2 reflects production, delivery to lungs (CO) and ventilation; normal 35–45 mmHg; a–Et gap 2–5 Waveform phases: I baseline, II rapid rise, III plateau, 0 inspiration Applications Tube placement, CPR quality (> 20 mmHg) and ROSC, ventilation monitoring, transport Dead space and PE, sedation, cardiac output trend Abnormal waveforms Sudden EtCO2 fall + normal shape + hypotension = low cardiac output/PE Zero: oesophageal intubation/disconnection; shark fin: bronchospasm; curare cleft: patient effort Rising baseline: rebreathing Sudden EtCO2 drop with hypotension = circulatory collapse until proven otherwise.

boxes.t: Ventilator-induced lung injury and oxygen targets
boxes.x: VILI mechanisms Volutrauma (overdistension), barotrauma, atelectrauma (opening/closing), biotrauma (cytokines) Ergotrauma: mechanical power (RR, Vt, pressures, flow) Ventilator changes Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤ 30, driving pressure ≤ 15, adequate PEEP, lower RR if possible Oxygen toxicity Free radicals, absorption atelectasis, tracheobronchitis, hypercapnia Target SpO2 92–96% / PaO2 8–10 kPa; avoid hyperoxia (ICU-ROX, HOT-ICU, Mega-ROX) Gentle ventilation and enough (not too much) oxygen protect the lung.

Classification Trigger: ineffective efforts, auto-triggering, double triggering, reverse triggering Flow: flow starvation; cycle: premature or delayed cycling Causes and fixes Ineffective efforts: auto-PEEP, high support → reduce Vt/support, add PEEP Double triggering: Vt too small/short Ti → increase Ti or Vt Delayed cycling (COPD): raise cycle-off % (40–50%) Sedation and new modes Treat pain/agitation; deep sedation masks, not fixes PAV+ and NAVA improve synchrony; NMB only if severe ARDS Look at the waveforms before you increase sedation.

Indications and timing Prolonged MV, weaning failure, airway protection, secretions, upper airway obstruction Benefits: comfort, less sedation, oral hygiene, faster weaning TracMan: early (≤ 4 days) vs late (≥ 10 days): no mortality difference Complications Early: bleeding, displacement, pneumothorax, surgical emphysema Late: stenosis, tracheo-innominate fistula, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, infection Emergency (NTSP algorithm) Call help, O2 to face and stoma; remove speaking valve/inner tube; pass suction catheter Not patent: deflate cuff → remove tube → oxygenate via face/stoma → reintubate orally or stoma A blocked trach: remove the inner tube first, then the trach if needed.

Risk classes (ESC) High: shock/arrest; intermediate-high: RV dysfunction + raised troponin; intermediate-low; low (sPESI 0) Work-up: CTPA (or bedside echo if unstable), troponin, BNP, leg ultrasound Reperfusion High-risk: systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg/2 h, or 0.6 mg/kg bolus in arrest) Intermediate-high: anticoagulate; rescue lysis if deterioration (PEITHO) Catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy if lysis contraindicated/fails; PERT RV support Avoid large fluids, noradrenaline for MAP, dobutamine, inhaled NO Avoid intubation if possible (RV collapse); VA-ECMO as rescue In massive PE, don't fill the failing RV: give pressor and reperfuse.

Diagnosis Fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension, ≥ 3 organ involvements, desquamation 1–2 weeks later Staphylococcal: tampons, wounds, blood cultures often negative, rash prominent Streptococcal: soft-tissue infection, pain, bacteraemia common, higher mortality Management Remove source (tampon), drain/debride, fluids and vasopressors Clindamycin (toxin suppression) + anti-staph agent (flucloxacillin/vancomycin) Consider IVIG in severe/refractory cases Organ dysfunction AKI, liver, DIC/thrombocytopenia, ARDS, encephalopathy, myositis (CK) Superantigen shock: add clindamycin and remove the source.

Diagnosis and risks DKA/uncontrolled diabetes, steroids, neutropenia, iron overload, COVID-19 Black eschar, facial swelling, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, cranial nerve palsy Confirmation Tissue biopsy: broad ribbon-like aseptate hyphae (right-angle branching), culture CT/MRI for orbital and cerebral spread Management Liposomal amphotericin B 5–10 mg/kg/day + urgent surgical debridement Correct DKA/acidosis, stop steroids, isavuconazole/posaconazole step-down Mucormycosis kills fast: biopsy, amphotericin and debridement without delay.

Definition and staging SBP < 90 (or vasopressor) + hypoperfusion (lactate > 2, oliguria, cold) from cardiac failure; CI < 2.2 SCAI stages A–E: at risk, beginning, classic, deteriorating, extremis Immediate management Emergency revascularisation of culprit only (CULPRIT-SHOCK) Noradrenaline for MAP 65; dobutamine (or milrinone) if low CO; avoid excessive fluid Echo, PA catheter in refractory shock; ventilation, RRT if needed Mechanical support IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit; DanGer Shock 2024: Impella CP ↓ mortality in STEMI shock ECLS-SHOCK: VA-ECMO no benefit, more bleeding; shock team decision Revascularise the culprit fast; use devices selectively with a shock team.

boxes.t: Mechanical circulatory support: IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO
boxes.x: Devices IABP: inflates in diastole (↑ coronary flow), deflates before systole (↓ afterload); +0.5 L/min Impella: axial pump LV → aorta, unloads LV, 2.5–5.5 L/min VA-ECMO: full biventricular + respiratory support; ↑ LV afterload Choice LV failure with adequate oxygenation: Impella; biventricular failure/arrest/hypoxia: VA-ECMO Combine ECMO + Impella (ECPELLA) to vent the LV VA-ECMO complications Bleeding, limb ischaemia (distal perfusion cannula), stroke, haemolysis, infection LV distension/pulmonary oedema; Harlequin (north–south) syndrome: right radial ABG Match the device to the failing ventricle and oxygenation.

Classification Warm/cold (perfusion) × wet/dry (congestion): warm-wet most common Phenotypes: acute decompensated, pulmonary oedema, RV failure, cardiogenic shock Management Warm-wet: IV furosemide (≥ 1–2.5× home dose), nitrates if SBP > 110, CPAP/NIV Cold-wet: inotrope ± vasopressor, then diuretics; find precipitant (CHAMPIT) Start/continue GDMT once stable (STRONG-HF) Inotropes and vasodilators Dobutamine/milrinone: short-term only, arrhythmia and mortality signal Levosimendan (calcium sensitiser): no mortality benefit (SURVIVE, LIDO) Treat congestion with diuretics + NIV; inotropes only for low output.

Classification (4th universal definition) Type 1 plaque rupture; type 2 supply–demand mismatch (sepsis, anaemia, tachycardia) Type 3 sudden death; 4 PCI-related; 5 CABG-related; myocardial injury = troponin without ischaemia NSTEMI management DAPT, anticoagulation, statin, beta-blocker; GRACE score Invasive within 24 h if high risk; immediate (< 2 h) if unstable/refractory pain Thrombocytopenia Heparin (HIT), GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors (acute, within hours), sepsis, dilution Use 4T score; switch to bivalirudin/argatroban if HIT Complications of STEMI Arrhythmia, heart failure/shock, mechanical rupture, pericarditis, LV thrombus In ICU most troponin rises are type 2 or injury: treat the cause.

Types (days 3–7) Ventricular septal rupture: new harsh murmur, step-up in O2 saturation (RV) Papillary muscle rupture: acute MR, flash pulmonary oedema, soft/absent murmur Free wall rupture: tamponade, PEA, sudden death Haemodynamic management Afterload reduction (nitroprusside if BP allows), IABP/Impella, VA-ECMO bridge Inotropes, ventilation, avoid excessive vasopressors Surgery and prognosis Urgent surgery for all; delay (bridge on MCS) may improve tissue repair Mortality 40–80%; percutaneous VSR closure option New murmur + shock after MI = mechanical complication: echo now.

Diagnosis Hypotension, tachycardia, rising CVP, falling then stopped drain output, low UO Echo may show localised clot (TOE); equalised pressures; pulsus paradoxus Immediate management Fluid, inotrope, avoid high PEEP; correct coagulopathy Re-sternotomy (bedside if arrest); pericardiocentesis for effusion in other settings Tamponade vs constriction Tamponade: pulsus paradoxus, Y descent absent, diastolic collapse Constriction: Kussmaul's sign, prominent Y descent, pericardial knock, thick pericardium Sudden fall in drain output with shock after cardiac surgery = tamponade.

Definition ≥ 3 episodes of sustained VT/VF or appropriate ICD shocks in 24 h Precipitants: ischaemia, heart failure, electrolytes, drugs (QT), thyroid, infection Acute management Defibrillation/ACLS, correct K > 4.5, Mg > 1, treat ischaemia Amiodarone + beta-blocker (propranolol); lidocaine; sedation/intubation Stellate ganglion block, catheter ablation, MCS as bridge Polymorphic VT Long QT (torsades): magnesium 2 g, stop drugs, overdrive pacing/isoprenaline Normal QT: treat ischaemia (angiography) Sedation and sympathetic blockade calm the electrical storm.

Causes and significance Sepsis, catecholamines, electrolytes, hypovolaemia, inflammation, atrial stretch, surgery Associated with ↑ mortality, stroke, longer stay Rate/rhythm control Correct K/Mg, reduce catecholamines where possible Unstable: synchronised DC cardioversion; amiodarone first-line in shock Beta-blocker (esmolol/landiolol) if BP allows; digoxin adjunct; avoid diltiazem in low EF Anticoagulation CHA2DS2-VASc vs bleeding risk; often reverts in ICU; consider if persists > 48 h Weigh bleeding (HAS-BLED) and procedures Fix the trigger first: many ICU AF episodes revert spontaneously.

Definitions Emergency: severe BP (often > 180/120) + acute organ damage; urgency: no organ damage Organs: brain, heart, aorta, kidney, eyes, placenta BP targets Reduce MAP ≤ 25% in first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 h, normal over 24–48 h Exceptions: aortic dissection (SBP < 120 within 20 min), ICH (SBP 140), stroke for lysis (< 185/110), eclampsia IV agents Labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine, esmolol, GTN (coronary/pulmonary oedema) Sodium nitroprusside: potent, cyanide toxicity; phentolamine for catecholamine crisis Lower BP gradually except in dissection: too fast causes ischaemia.

Pathophysiology Failed cerebral autoregulation → vasogenic oedema; endothelial dysfunction Posterior circulation (poor sympathetic innervation) most affected Causes and triggers Hypertension, eclampsia, renal failure, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus), chemotherapy, SLE, sepsis Management Lower BP gradually; stop offending drug; treat seizures (levetiracetam) MRI: parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema (FLAIR); magnesium in eclampsia Prognosis Usually reversible in days–weeks; poor with haemorrhage, cytotoxic oedema, delayed treatment Headache + seizures + visual loss with high BP or tacrolimus → MRI for PRES.

Classification Stanford A (ascending, surgery) / B (descending, mostly medical); DeBakey I–III Includes intramural haematoma and penetrating aortic ulcer Medical management IV beta-blocker first (esmolol/labetalol) → HR < 60, then SBP < 120 Analgesia; vasodilator after beta-blockade Definitive Type A: emergency surgery; type B complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/BP): TEVAR Complications Tamponade, AR, MI, stroke, mesenteric/renal/limb ischaemia, paraplegia Rate control before vasodilators in aortic dissection.

Features and diagnosis Paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations, hypertension; crisis with surgery/anaesthesia Plasma free or urinary metanephrines, then CT/MRI, MIBG/PET Crisis management Alpha-blockade first (phentolamine bolus, then infusion); magnesium, nicardipine Beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade (avoid unopposed alpha) After removal/stopping trigger: profound hypotension → fluids, vasopressors; hypoglycaemia Elective preparation Phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin 10–14 days, then beta-blocker; liberal salt and fluid Never beta-block before alpha-block in phaeochromocytoma.

Selection Witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, shockable rhythm, age < 70, no-flow < 5 min, low-flow < 60 min Reversible cause, no major comorbidity, EtCO2 > 10, arrival within 60 min Evidence ARREST 2020: survival 43% vs 7% (stopped early) Prague OHCA: no significant benefit; INCEPTION: no benefit (system dependent) Contraindications Unwitnessed, prolonged no-flow, terminal illness, aortic dissection, severe AR, frailty Post-ECPR care Coronary angiography, LV venting, limb perfusion, temperature control, neuroprognostication ECPR works in selected patients within well-trained systems.

boxes.t: High-quality CPR, reversible causes and POCUS
boxes.x: High-quality CPR 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, full recoil, pauses < 10 s, rotate every 2 min Adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min; amiodarone 300 mg after 3rd shock EtCO2 > 20 mmHg good CPR; sudden rise suggests ROSC Reversible causes (4 Hs, 4 Ts) Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia Thrombosis (coronary/PE), tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins POCUS during arrest Only in pulse checks (< 10 s); identifies tamponade, RV dilatation, hypovolaemia, pseudo-PEA Minimise pauses: every second without compressions lowers survival.

Emergency angiography STEMI after ROSC: immediate; no STEMI: delayed approach as good (COACT, TOMAHAWK) Post-cardiac arrest syndrome Brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, systemic ischaemia–reperfusion (SIRS-like), persistent cause Targets MAP ≥ 65 (no benefit from higher: BOX), SpO2 94–98%, normocapnia (PaCO2 4.5–6) Fever avoidance ≤ 37.7 for 72 h, glucose 6–10, treat seizures Post-arrest care: avoid hypoxia, hypotension, hyperthermia.

Evolution of evidence 2002 HACA & Bernard: 32–34 °C improved outcome TTM-1 2013: 33 = 36 °C; HYPERION 2019: 33 benefit in non-shockable TTM-2 2021: 33 °C = normothermia with fever control Current: prevent fever (≤ 37.7 °C) for at least 72 h Practical delivery Surface or intravascular devices with feedback; sedation; control shivering (BSAS) Monitor K, glucose, coagulation, bradycardia Neuroprotection ↓ Metabolic rate, excitotoxicity, free radicals, apoptosis, BBB disruption Fever is harmful after cardiac arrest: control temperature, not depth.

Timing ≥ 72 h after ROSC after sedation is cleared; multimodal Predictors of poor outcome (ERC 2021) Absent pupillary + corneal reflexes ≥ 72 h; bilateral absent N20 SSEPs NSE > 60 µg/L at 48–72 h; status myoclonus ≤ 72 h; malignant EEG CT diffuse oedema (low GWR); MRI diffusion restriction Family communication Honest, consistent, uncertainty explained, regular meetings, involve team Never prognosticate from a single test: use ≥ 2 concordant findings.

boxes.t: Mechanical CPR, survival factors and arrest drugs
boxes.x: Mechanical devices LUCAS, AutoPulse: no better survival (LINC, PARAMEDIC, CIRC) Useful in transport, PCI lab, prolonged CPR, ECPR bridge Survival factors Witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, early defibrillation (public AED), shockable rhythm Short time to ROSC, good post-arrest care in cardiac arrest centres Drugs Adrenaline: ↑ ROSC and survival, not good neurology (PARAMEDIC2) Amiodarone/lidocaine ↑ survival to admission (ALPS); no routine calcium, bicarbonate Chain of survival: early CPR and early shock matter most.

Causes Ischaemia (inferior MI), drugs (beta-blockers, CCB, digoxin), hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism Hypoxia, raised ICP, hypothermia, vagal stimulation Immediate management Atropine 500 µg IV (max 3 mg); adrenaline/isoprenaline infusion Transcutaneous then transvenous pacing; treat cause AV block types 1st degree: PR > 200 ms; Mobitz I: progressive PR prolongation Mobitz II: sudden dropped QRS (needs pacing); 3rd: AV dissociation Mobitz II and complete heart block need pacing.

Why CVP fails Static pressure ≠ volume; affected by RV function, PEEP, valves, IAP Dynamic tests PLR: ↑ CO ≥ 10% (works in AF/spontaneous breathing) PPV/SVV > 12–13% (need controlled ventilation, Vt ≥ 8, sinus rhythm) End-expiratory occlusion ↑ CO 5%, mini-fluid challenge, IVC variation Monitoring tools Echo: bedside, function; PiCCO: CO, EVLW, GEDV; PA catheter: RV failure, PAP, SvO2 Pulse contour devices for continuous CO Fluid only if responsive and still hypoperfused.

boxes.t: AKI: KDIGO, biomarkers and care bundle
boxes.x: Definition and stages Creatinine ↑ ≥ 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) in 48 h, or ≥ 1.5× baseline in 7 days, or UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h ≥ 6 h Stage 1: 1.5–1.9×; stage 2: 2–2.9× or oliguria ≥ 12 h; stage 3: ≥ 3×, Cr ≥ 4 mg/dL, RRT, anuria ≥ 12 h Causes Pre-renal, renal (ATN, AIN, GN), post-renal; sepsis most common in ICU New biomarkers TIMP-2 × IGFBP7 (NephroCheck) > 0.3: stress; NGAL, KIM-1, cystatin C, L-FABP Detect injury before creatinine rises; guide KDIGO bundle (PrevAKI) KDIGO bundle Stop nephrotoxins, optimise volume and MAP, monitor Cr/UO, avoid hyperglycaemia, avoid contrast Biomarkers flag the stressed kidney early: act with the bundle.

Solute removal Diffusion (CVVHD, small molecules), convection (CVVH, middle molecules), combined (CVVHDF) Ultrafiltration for fluid removal Dose Delivered effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h (prescribe 25–30); RENAL & ATN: higher dose no benefit Anticoagulation Regional citrate first line (KDIGO): longer filter life, less bleeding (RICH) Citrate toxicity: total/ionised Ca ratio > 2.5; heparin if citrate contraindicated (liver failure) Prolonging filter life Good catheter (right IJ, femoral), pre-dilution, blood flow 150–250, minimise interruptions Citrate is the standard: watch the Ca ratio for accumulation.

Absolute indications (AEIOU) Refractory acidosis (pH < 7.15), K > 6.5 despite treatment, uraemic complications Fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics, dialysable toxins Timing evidence ELAIN: early benefit (single centre); AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU: no benefit early STARRT-AKI: accelerated = standard; more RRT dependence early AKIKI-2: very delayed harmful Decision Watchful waiting if no urgent indication; furosemide stress test (< 200 mL/2 h predicts progression) Start for complications, not creatinine alone; avoid too-late.

Definition and risks Creatinine rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL or ≥ 1.5× within 48–72 h after contrast Risks: CKD (eGFR < 30), diabetes, hypovolaemia, heart failure, high dose, intra-arterial Prevention IV isotonic fluids (saline/bicarbonate) before and after; stop nephrotoxins/metformin Lowest dose of iso-/low-osmolar contrast; NAC not effective (PRESERVE) Pathophysiology Renal vasoconstriction (medullary hypoxia), direct tubular toxicity, viscosity, ROS Don't withhold needed contrast: hydrate and minimise volume.

Comparison ATN: ischaemic/toxic (sepsis, aminoglycosides), muddy brown casts AIN: drugs (PPI, beta-lactams, NSAIDs), infection; fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts Urinary indices Pre-renal: FeNa < 1%, FeUrea < 35%, urine Na < 20, osmolality > 500 ATN: FeNa > 2%, urine osmolality < 350; diuretics affect FeNa Drug-induced AIN Stop offending drug; steroids if no improvement in 3–5 days Biopsy if unclear Fever + rash + eosinophilia after a new drug → think AIN.

HRS-AKI criteria (ICA) Cirrhosis + ascites, AKI by ICA criteria, no response after 48 h albumin 1 g/kg No shock, nephrotoxins, structural kidney damage Pathophysiology Splanchnic vasodilatation (NO) → ↓ effective volume → RAAS/SNS activation → renal vasoconstriction Management Stop diuretics/NSAIDs, treat precipitant (SBP, bleeding) Terlipressin + albumin (CONFIRM); noradrenaline in ICU; midodrine + octreotide if neither Definitive treatment Liver transplantation; TIPS selected; RRT as bridge Terlipressin + albumin is first-line; transplant is definitive.

Classification Type 1 acute cardiac → AKI; 2 chronic cardiac → CKD; 3 acute renal → cardiac Type 4 chronic renal → cardiac; 5 systemic (sepsis) Pathophysiology Venous congestion ↑ renal venous pressure, low output, neurohormonal activation Diuretic resistance Double loop dose, infusion; sequential nephron blockade (thiazide, acetazolamide: ADVOR) Spot urine Na < 50–70 mmol/L at 2 h → escalate Ultrafiltration if refractory Congestion, not low output, drives most cardiorenal AKI.

Causes Trauma/crush, immobility, seizures, exertion, hyperthermia, drugs (statins), toxins, infections Electrolytes: hypoK, hypoP Pathophysiology Myoglobin: tubular obstruction, direct toxicity (haem iron, ROS), vasoconstriction Worse in acidic urine and hypovolaemia Management Aggressive IV fluids (UO 200–300 mL/h); bicarbonate/mannitol not proven Treat hyperkalaemia; RRT for refractory complications Complications Hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia (early) → hypercalcaemia (recovery), compartment syndrome, DIC CK > 5000 → protect the kidney with early fluids.

Cairo–Bishop definition Lab: ≥ 2 of urate, K, phosphate ↑ (or 25% rise) and Ca ↓, within 3 days before to 7 days after therapy Clinical: lab TLS + AKI, arrhythmia, seizure or death Emergency management Hydration 3 L/m²/day; rasburicase (avoid in G6PD) Treat hyperkalaemia; avoid calcium unless symptomatic; early RRT Prevention Allopurinol (low–intermediate risk); rasburicase in high risk TLS is preventable: hydrate and lower urate before chemotherapy.

Principle Removes plasma (antibodies, toxins) and replaces with albumin or FFP (TTP) 1–1.5 plasma volumes per session ASFA category I TTP, GBS, myasthenic crisis, anti-GBM, CIDP, hyperviscosity, catastrophic APS Complications Hypocalcaemia (citrate), hypotension, bleeding (fibrinogen loss), infection, catheter problems Remove highly protein-bound drugs; give doses after session TTP is the classic urgent indication: start without delay.

Calculations AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3), normal 8–12; correct for albumin (+2.5 per 10 g/L fall) Osmolar gap = measured − (2Na + glucose + urea), > 10 suggests toxic alcohol Delta ratio: < 1 additional NAGMA; > 2 metabolic alkalosis Causes (GOLD MARK) Glycols, oxoproline (paracetamol), L-lactate, D-lactate, methanol, aspirin, renal failure, ketones Management Treat cause; fomepizole/ethanol + dialysis for toxic alcohols Bicarbonate only if pH < 7.1–7.2 with AKI Calculate the AG and osmolar gap in every metabolic acidosis.

boxes.t: Normal anion gap acidosis and RTA
boxes.x: Urinary anion gap UAG = Na + K − Cl; negative = GI loss (NH4 excreted); positive = RTA RTA types Type 1 (distal): urine pH > 5.5, low K, stones Type 2 (proximal): bicarbonate wasting, Fanconi, low K Type 4: hyperkalaemic, hypoaldosteronism (diabetes, drugs) Management Bicarbonate or citrate (type 1, 2); fludrocortisone/K reduction (type 4) Avoid excessive saline (hyperchloraemia) Negative UAG means GI loss; positive means renal.

Interpretation Acute: HCO3 ↑ 1 per 10 mmHg PaCO2 rise; chronic: ↑ 3.5–4 Alkalosis: acute HCO3 ↓ 2; chronic ↓ 4–5 Respiratory acidosis management Treat cause (COPD, sedation, neuromuscular), NIV, intubation if fails Avoid overcorrection (post-hypercapnic alkalosis) Effects of severe acidosis ↓ Contractility, arrhythmias, vasodilation, ↑ ICP, hyperkalaemia, insulin resistance Check compensation to classify acute vs chronic.

Approach Serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine Na, volume status SIADH: low serum osm, urine osm > 100, urine Na > 30, euvolaemic Severe symptomatic 3% saline 150 mL over 20 min, repeat ×2–3; target ↑ 4–6 mmol/L Max 10 mmol/L in 24 h (8 if high risk) Osmotic demyelination Dysarthria, quadriparesis after 2–6 days; risk: alcohol, malnutrition, hypoK Overcorrection: D5W + DDAVP to re-lower Treat severe symptoms fast, then limit total correction.

Causes Water loss (renal: DI, osmotic diuresis; extra-renal: GI, skin), hypotonic loss Sodium gain (hypertonic saline, bicarbonate) Water deficit Deficit = TBW × (Na/140 − 1); TBW = 0.6 × weight (0.5 women/elderly) Correct ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/day in chronic; enteral water or D5W Diabetes insipidus Polyuria, dilute urine (< 300 mOsm/kg) Central: DDAVP response; nephrogenic: thiazide, NSAID, stop lithium Calculate the deficit, add ongoing losses, correct slowly.

ECG and causes Peaked T, flattened P, wide QRS, sine wave, VF Causes: AKI, drugs (ACEI, spironolactone), rhabdo, acidosis, TLS Emergency treatment Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL (stabilises myocardium) Insulin 10 U + 25 g glucose; salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised Bicarbonate if acidotic; remove K: SZC, patiromer, dialysis Shifting wears off Insulin/salbutamol last 4–6 h → rebound; need removal (dialysis) Calcium protects the heart, but only removal fixes the potassium.

Causes Shift (insulin, beta-agonists, alkalosis, thyrotoxicosis) Losses: GI (diarrhoea), renal (diuretics, RTA, hyperaldosteronism), low Mg Periodic paralysis Familial or thyrotoxic; rapid shift after carbohydrate/exercise Small K doses (10 mEq/h) to avoid rebound; propranolol for thyrotoxic Replacement IV KCl 10–20 mmol/h (central if > 10); correct Mg Monitor ECG and levels In periodic paralysis, K is shifted not lost: replace gently.

Hypercalcaemia PTH high: primary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism PTH low: malignancy (PTHrP, bone mets), vitamin D, granulomas, thyrotoxicosis Severe management IV saline 200–300 mL/h, then calcitonin; zoledronate; denosumab if CKD Dialysis if refractory Hypocalcaemia Causes: low Mg, sepsis, citrate, post-parathyroidectomy, pancreatitis Calcium gluconate 10–20 mL 10% IV over 10 min, then infusion; correct Mg Rehydrate first in hypercalcaemia; correct Mg in hypocalcaemia.

Generation and maintenance Generation: H+ loss (vomiting, NGT), diuretics, alkali load Maintenance: hypovolaemia, Cl depletion, hypoK, hyperaldosteronism Urine chloride Cl < 20: chloride responsive (vomiting, diuretics after) Cl > 20: chloride resistant (hyperaldosteronism, Bartter, Gitelman) Management Saline + KCl for Cl-responsive; acetazolamide if fluid overloaded HCl infusion rare; treat aldosterone excess Most ICU metabolic alkalosis responds to Cl and K.

boxes.t: Systematic ABG and the Stewart approach
boxes.x: Systematic interpretation pH → primary disorder → compensation (Winter: PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2) AG (albumin-corrected) → delta ratio → oxygenation (A–a gradient) Stewart approach Independent variables: PaCO2, SID (Na + K − Cl − lactate), weak acids (albumin, phosphate) Low SID → acidosis (hyperchloraemia); low albumin → alkalosis Value Explains saline acidosis and hypoalbuminaemia; SIG reveals unmeasured anions Stewart adds insight in ICU acidosis: check SID and albumin.

boxes.t: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: grading and early care
boxes.x: Grading WFNS (GCS ± motor deficit, I–V); Hunt & Hess I–V Modified Fisher (CT blood thickness + IVH, 0–4): predicts vasospasm Before securing the aneurysm SBP < 160 (labetalol, nicardipine); analgesia, antiemetics Nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days; EVD for hydrocephalus Secure early (< 24–72 h): coiling preferred (ISAT) or clipping Complications Neuro: rebleeding, hydrocephalus, DCI, seizures Systemic: neurogenic pulmonary oedema, Takotsubo, arrhythmia, hyponatraemia Secure the aneurysm early: rebleeding is the first killer.

DCI New focal deficit or ↓ GCS ≥ 2 for ≥ 1 h (days 4–14), not explained otherwise Vasospasm (TCD velocities > 120 cm/s, Lindegaard > 3) is one cause; microthrombi, CSD Management Euvolaemia, nimodipine; induced hypertension if DCI Endovascular: intra-arterial vasodilators, angioplasty; avoid prophylactic HHH therapy Hyponatraemia SIADH (euvolaemic) vs cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic, high urine Na + volume) Do not fluid restrict in SAH; saline/hypertonic, fludrocortisone for CSW Never fluid restrict in SAH: hypovolaemia worsens DCI.

ILAE definition Convulsive: t1 = 5 min (treat), t2 = 30 min (damage) Focal impaired awareness: t1 10 min, t2 60 min Time-based management 0–5 min: ABC, glucose, thiamine 5–20: benzodiazepine (lorazepam 4 mg IV, midazolam 10 mg IM/buccal), repeat once 20–40: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (ESETT: equal) > 40: anaesthetic (propofol, midazolam, thiopental) + EEG Systemic complications Hypoxia, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, arrhythmia, neurogenic oedema Give an adequate benzodiazepine dose early; delay makes it refractory.

Definitions Refractory: fails benzodiazepine + second-line; super-refractory: ≥ 24 h despite anaesthesia NORSE: new-onset refractory SE without cause (autoimmune, FIRES) Super-refractory management Continuous EEG; anaesthetic to burst suppression 24–48 h, slow wean Ketamine, add other ASMs, steroids/IVIG/PLEX if autoimmune, ketogenic diet NCSE Unexplained coma or fluctuating consciousness, subtle twitching EEG required (Salzburg criteria); treat like SE Unexplained coma after seizures → EEG for NCSE.

ICH score (0–6) GCS 3–4 (2), 5–12 (1); volume ≥ 30 mL (1); IVH (1); infratentorial (1); age ≥ 80 (1) Score 3 ≈ 72% 30-day mortality; don't use alone to limit care Acute management SBP 140 (INTERACT2/3), avoid falls > 70 mmHg; reverse anticoagulation (PCC, idarucizumab, andexanet) Glucose, temperature, seizures if clinical, VTE prevention with IPC Surgery Cerebellar > 3 cm or brainstem compression/hydrocephalus: evacuate Lobar superficial clots: MIS (ENRICH); EVD for hydrocephalus Bundle care (BP, glucose, temperature, reversal) improves ICH outcome.

boxes.t: TBI: secondary injury and BTF targets
boxes.x: Injury types Primary: at impact; secondary: hypoxia, hypotension, raised ICP, hyper/hypocapnia, fever, seizures, glucose Immediate management Intubate if GCS ≤ 8; SpO2 > 94%, PaCO2 4.5–5 kPa SBP ≥ 100 (50–69 yr) or ≥ 110 (15–49, > 70); CT; neurosurgery BTF targets ICP < 22 mmHg, CPP 60–70, Na 140–145, glucose 6–10, temp < 38 Seizure prophylaxis 7 days (levetiracetam/phenytoin) One episode of hypotension or hypoxia doubles TBI mortality.

boxes.t: Raised ICP: Monro–Kellie, SIBICC and osmotherapy
boxes.x: Monro–Kellie Fixed skull: brain + blood + CSF; compensation then steep rise on pressure–volume curve SIBICC tiers Tier 0–1: head up, sedation, normocapnia, EVD drainage, osmotherapy Tier 2: mild hypocapnia (4.3–4.6 kPa), NMB, MAP challenge Tier 3: barbiturate coma, decompressive craniectomy (RESCUEicp), hypothermia Mannitol vs hypertonic saline Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg: osmotic diuresis, hypotension; check osmolar gap HTS 3%/23.4%: volume expansion, no diuresis, hypernatraemia risk Escalate in tiers; HTS preferred if hypovolaemic.

IV thrombolysis Within 4.5 h (or wake-up with DWI–FLAIR mismatch); tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg BP < 185/110 before, < 180/105 for 24 h after Contraindications: haemorrhage, recent surgery/bleeding, platelets < 100, INR > 1.7 Thrombectomy LVO within 6 h; up to 24 h with mismatch (DAWN, DEFUSE-3); large core (SELECT2) Post-reperfusion care Neuro checks, BP, glucose, temperature, swallow, haemorrhagic transformation (CT at 24 h) Time is brain: door-to-needle < 60 min.

Malignant MCA > 50% MCA territory, early deterioration from oedema (days 2–5) Decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 h in ≤ 60 yr (DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET); DESTINY II > 60 Medical measures Head up, normothermia, glucose, osmotherapy as bridge, avoid hypotonic fluids TIA ABCD2 limits; urgent imaging, carotid Doppler, ECG monitoring DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel 21 days) for minor stroke/TIA (CHANCE, POINT) Early hemicraniectomy saves life in malignant MCA infarction.

boxes.t: Spinal cord injury and neurogenic shock
boxes.x: ASIA classification A complete; B sensory incomplete; C motor incomplete < 3; D motor ≥ 3; E normal Neurogenic vs spinal shock Neurogenic: hypotension + bradycardia (loss of sympathetic tone, injury above T6) Spinal shock: flaccid areflexia temporarily below injury MAP 85–90 for 5–7 days; noradrenaline; atropine/pacing for bradycardia Respiratory management C3–5: diaphragm; monitor VC (< 15 mL/kg → intubate); early tracheostomy Lesions above C5 often need ventilation: monitor VC closely.

Diagnosis Ascending flaccid weakness, areflexia; CSF high protein, normal cells Variants: AIDP, AMAN/AMSAN, Miller Fisher (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) Intubation (20/30/40 rule) VC < 20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30 cmH2O, MEP < 40 Bulbar dysfunction, rapid progression, autonomic instability Treatment IVIG 0.4 g/kg × 5 days or plasma exchange (equal); no steroids VTE prophylaxis, pain, autonomic monitoring, physio Measure VC serially: don't wait for hypoxia.

Myasthenic crisis Respiratory failure from MG weakness; triggers: infection, surgery, drugs (aminoglycosides, Mg) Differentiate Cholinergic: excess pyridostigmine, miosis, salivation, bradycardia, fasciculations Myasthenic: no muscarinic signs; ice pack test; EMG Management Intubate if VC < 20 mL/kg; stop pyridostigmine while ventilated IVIG or plasma exchange, then steroids/immunosuppression Avoid aminoglycosides and NMB drugs in MG.

Respiratory and cardiac Restrictive lung disease, weak cough, sleep hypoventilation; FVC falls Dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias ICU respiratory care NIV early, mechanical insufflation–exsufflation (cough assist), extubate to NIV Anaesthetic concerns Avoid suxamethonium (hyperkalaemia, rhabdo) and volatile agents TIVA, careful NMB use, cardiac assessment Suxamethonium can kill DMD patients: never use it.

Definition Episodic tachycardia, hypertension, fever, sweating, posturing after brain injury (TBI) Disconnection of inhibitory pathways → excitatory reflexes Diagnosis PSH-AM score (clinical features + diagnosis likelihood) Exclude sepsis, withdrawal, seizures Management Avoid triggers; opioids, gabapentin, propranolol, clonidine Bromocriptine, intrathecal baclofen PSH is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out sepsis first.

First hour Blood cultures, dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly (pneumococcus), ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly Add ampicillin (> 50 yr, Listeria), vancomycin if resistance; acyclovir if encephalitis CT before LP Focal signs, GCS < 10, seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromise CSF comparison Bacterial: high neutrophils, protein > 1 g/L, glucose < 40% Viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose; TB: lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose Never delay antibiotics for CT or LP.

Definition Infection of ventricles after EVD/surgery: CSF pleocytosis, low glucose, positive culture Risks: EVD > 5 days, frequent sampling, CSF leak, IVH Management Vancomycin + meropenem/cefepime; intraventricular antibiotics if refractory Remove/replace device EVD prevention Aseptic insertion, tunnelling, antibiotic-impregnated catheters, limit sampling, closed system Limit EVD sampling and duration to prevent ventriculitis.

Diagnosis Fever, confusion, seizures, focal signs CSF HSV PCR, MRI temporal lobe changes, EEG periodic discharges Treatment IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for 14–21 days; start empirically Adjust for renal function; repeat PCR Complications Seizures, memory loss, autoimmune NMDA encephalitis later; mortality ~ 70% untreated Start acyclovir empirically in encephalitis: don't wait.

boxes.t: ICU delirium and the ABCDEF bundle
boxes.x: Diagnosis CAM-ICU: acute onset/fluctuation + inattention + (altered LOC or disorganised thinking) ICDSC ≥ 4 Risk factors and consequences Age, dementia, sepsis, benzodiazepines, sleep loss ↑ Mortality, long-term cognitive impairment, longer stay ABCDEF bundle Assess pain, SAT + SBT, choice of sedation, delirium monitoring, early mobility, family Haloperidol not effective (AID-ICU), dexmedetomidine for agitation Prevent delirium: light sedation, mobility, sleep, family.

Principles Analgesia first, light sedation (RASS 0 to −2), daily awakening Drugs Propofol: rapid offset, hypotension Dexmedetomidine: rousable, less delirium, bradycardia (MENDS2, SPICE III) Benzodiazepines: more delirium, accumulation → avoid Propofol infusion syndrome > 4 mg/kg/h > 48 h; metabolic acidosis, rhabdo, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia, AKI Stop propofol, supportive, RRT, ECMO Avoid benzodiazepines; watch propofol dose and lactate.

boxes.t: Brainstem death testing and donor management
boxes.x: Preconditions Known cause of irreversible brain damage; exclude sedation, hypothermia, metabolic/endocrine causes Temperature > 34 °C, MAP > 60, normal Na, glucose, PaCO2 Clinical tests Absent pupil, corneal, oculovestibular, gag, cough reflexes; no motor response to pain Apnoea test: PaCO2 rises > 6.65 kPa with pH < 7.4 and no breathing Donor management MAP > 60, DI with DDAVP, hormone replacement, protective ventilation Brain death needs strict preconditions before testing.

Risk stratification Glasgow–Blatchford (pre-endoscopy; 0–1 → outpatient), Rockall (post-endoscopy) Forrest classification of ulcer stigmata (Ia spurting → III clean base) Resuscitation Restrictive transfusion: Hb 7 g/dL (8 if cardiac disease) IV PPI, erythromycin before endoscopy; correct coagulopathy; stop NSAIDs/aspirin review Endoscopy and beyond Endoscopy within 24 h (urgent if unstable) Dual therapy (adrenaline + clip/thermal) for Forrest Ia–IIb Rebleed: repeat endoscopy → interventional radiology embolisation → surgery TXA not beneficial (HALT-IT) Transfuse restrictively; endoscope within 24 h.

Before endoscopy Restrictive transfusion (Hb 7–8), avoid overfilling Terlipressin (or octreotide), antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g/day) Airway protection if encephalopathy/massive haematemesis Endoscopic and rescue therapy Band ligation (oesophageal); cyanoacrylate for gastric varices Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken) or self-expanding stent as bridge Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h in Child C 10–13 or B with active bleeding Rebleeding prevention Non-selective beta-blocker (carvedilol) + repeat banding Antibiotics + vasoactive drug + banding = standard bundle.

Definition Coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) + encephalopathy within 26 weeks, no prior liver disease O'Grady: hyperacute (< 7 d), acute (8–28 d), subacute (> 28 d) King's College criteria (paracetamol) pH < 7.3 after resuscitation, or all of: INR > 6.5, creatinine > 300 µmol/L, grade 3–4 HE Lactate > 3.5 (4 h) or > 3 (12 h) added ICU management NAC regardless of time; neuroprotection (Na 145–150, head up), glucose ICP concerns: high ammonia > 150; RRT early (lowers ammonia) Avoid FFP unless bleeding; refer early to transplant centre Refer early: deterioration is rapid.

Classification West Haven grades 1–4; type A (ALF), B (bypass), C (cirrhosis) Precipitants: infection, GI bleed, constipation, electrolytes, sedatives, dehydration Management Treat precipitant; lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day; rifaximin for recurrence Airway protection if grade 3–4 Ammonia High ammonia correlates with severity in ALF (> 150–200 → cerebral oedema) In cirrhosis, levels not useful for diagnosis/monitoring Look for the trigger in every episode of HE.

Definition Acute decompensation of cirrhosis + organ failures + high short-term mortality CLIF-C ACLF grades 1–3 Organ support Albumin for SBP/HRS, terlipressin; vasopressors (MAP ≥ 65) Restrictive transfusion; avoid nephrotoxins; nutrition Treat infection early; consider steroids for alcoholic hepatitis Prognosis ACLF-3: 28-day mortality > 70% Reassess at day 3–7; transplant evaluation; palliative care ACLF grade guides the ceiling of care discussion.

Interpretation Ascitic neutrophils > 250/mm³ = SBP; culture often negative SAAG ≥ 11 g/L = portal hypertension Management Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone (carbapenem if nosocomial) Albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3 ↓ HRS and mortality Prophylaxis: norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin after SBP Large-volume paracentesis Albumin 8 g/L removed when > 5 L (prevents paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction) Albumin with antibiotics in SBP reduces kidney injury.

boxes.t: Acute pancreatitis: severity and early care
boxes.x: Revised Atlanta Mild: no organ failure; moderate: transient OF < 48 h or local complications Severe: persistent OF > 48 h (modified Marshall) Early management Moderate goal-directed fluid (WATERFALL: aggressive harms) Analgesia (opioids OK), early enteral nutrition within 24–48 h No prophylactic antibiotics; ERCP within 24 h only for cholangitis Complications Systemic: ARDS, AKI, shock, ACS, hypocalcaemia Local: APFC, pseudocyst, ANC, WON, infected necrosis Organ failure duration defines severity.

Diagnosis Clinical deterioration after week 2; gas on CT; FNA rarely needed Management Carbapenem/quinolone + metronidazole Step-up approach: percutaneous or endoscopic drainage → necrosectomy (PANTER, TENSION) Delay intervention to ≥ 4 weeks (walled-off) (POINTER) Early surgery Abdominal compartment syndrome, bowel ischaemia, perforation, haemorrhage Step up and delay: minimally invasive first.

Timing and dose Early EN within 48 h if haemodynamically stable (low dose on vasopressors) Energy 70% of target first week (indirect calorimetry), protein 1.3 g/kg/day progressively EFFORT Protein: high protein no benefit (harm in AKI) Feed intolerance GRV > 500 mL: prokinetics (metoclopramide, erythromycin), post-pyloric Assess abdomen, constipation, ischaemia Parenteral nutrition If EN contraindicated/fails after 3–7 days; early PN if high risk/malnourished EPaNIC: late PN better Start enteral feeding early but slow; avoid overfeeding.

Pathophysiology Insulin surge → intracellular shift of phosphate, K, Mg; thiamine depletion Results: heart failure, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, Wernicke's High-risk (NICE) BMI < 16, weight loss > 15%, little intake > 10 days, low K/P/Mg before feeding Management Start 5–10 kcal/kg/day, increase over 4–7 days Thiamine before feeding; replace P, K, Mg; monitor daily Feed slowly and replace phosphate in high-risk patients.

boxes.t: Toxic megacolon and acute severe colitis
